refs.quote: MESTINON (pyridostigmine bromide) is an orally active cholinesterase inhibitor. Chemically, pyridostigmine bromide is 3-hydroxy-1-methylpyridinium bromide dimethylcarbamate.

tall_man.note: Not listed in FDA/ISMP Tall Man list; generic name lowercase per EXTRACTION.md

refs.quote: MESTINON is useful in the treatment of myasthenia gravis. === DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION === DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION: MESTINON is available in three dosage forms: Oral Solution - raspberry-flavored,
Conventional tablets - The average dose is ten 60 mg tablets or ten 5 mL teaspoonfuls daily, spaced to provide maximum relief when maximum strength is needed.

regimens.dose_text: Initial: 60 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours while awake. Adjust size and frequency of dose to clinical response. Average dose is 600 mg daily (ten 60 mg tablets). Timespan 180 mg 1-2 times daily may be used at bedtime for nocturnal/morning symptoms.

refs.quote: Pyridostigmine is mainly excreted unchanged by the kidney. 6,7,8 Therefore, lower doses may be required in patients with renal disease, and treatment should be based on titration of drug dosage to effect.

hepatic.value: No dosage adjustment provided in product labeling; primarily excreted unchanged by kidneys.

value.instructions: Conventional 60 mg tablets may be crushed; oral solution (60 mg/5 mL) is available and easily administered via tube. TIMESPAN extended-release tablets must NOT be crushed or chewed.

refs.quote: TIMESPAN tablets - each containing 180 mg pyridostigmine bromide.
ADVERSE REACTIONS: The side effects of MESTINON are most commonly related to overdosage and generally are of two varieties, muscarinic and nicotinic.

mechanism_of_action.value: Reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, prolonging the action of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction.

refs.quote: ACTIONS: MESTINON inhibits the destruction of acetylcholine by cholinesterase and thereby permits freer transmission of nerve impulses across the neuromuscular junction.

value.metabolism: hydrolyzed by cholinesterases; minor hepatic microsomal metabolism

value: Muscarinic gastrointestinal symptoms: abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, increased peristalsis
Increased salivation (sialorrhea) and increased bronchial secretions

refs.quote: Among those in the former group are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, increased peristalsis, increased salivation, increased bronchial secretions, miosis and diaphoresis.

value: Cholinergic Crisis (depolarizing neuromuscular blockade resulting in generalized flaccid muscle paralysis, respiratory failure, and apnea; must be differentiated from myasthenic crisis; requires immediate atropine and ventilatory support)
Severe nicotinic symptoms: prominent muscle fasciculations, muscle cramps, and profound muscle weakness
Severe bronchospasm, laryngospasm, and copious pulmonary secretions leading to airway obstruction (contraindicated in bronchial asthma)
Marked bradycardia, nodal rhythms, AV block, and syncope
Mechanical intestinal or urinary obstruction exacerbation (contraindicated)

refs.quote: Nicotinic side effects are comprised chiefly of muscle cramps, fasciculation and weakness.

value.effect: Atropine antagonizes muscarinic adverse effects of pyridostigmine but may mask early signs of cholinergic crisis, delaying recognition of life-threatening overdosage.
value.management: Care should be observed in the use of atropine for counteracting side effects; avoid routine masking of cholinergic overdose symptoms in myasthenia gravis.
